title: Dr. Reddy's Tech Transfer Redesign
projectLabel: Dr. Reddy's Laboratories • Service & Information Design • 2026
subtitle: A strategic overhaul of New Product Development handovers to reduce cognitive overload on the manufacturing floor.
pageTitle: Dr. Reddy's NPD Service Design | Areen Pednekar
metaDescription: A UX and service design case study detailing the redesign of Standard Operating Procedures to accelerate New Product Development and scale-up in pharmaceutical manufacturing.
previewText: Transforming dense compliance manuals into highly usable, action-oriented tools to accelerate pharmaceutical scale-up.
meta: Service Design, Systems Thinking, Cognitive Ergonomics, Information Architecture

presentationSections.label: Overview
presentationSections.content:
How do you prevent human error when transitioning a new drug from R&D to mass manufacturing?

In pharmaceutical New Product Development (NPD), the most vulnerable phase is Technology Transfer: the moment a new formulation moves from the R&D lab to the factory floor for Scale-Up. Manufacturing operators must learn and execute entirely new, highly complex procedures flawlessly.

At Dr. Reddy's, the artifact managing this transfer is the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP). These documents were written for regulatory auditors, not the humans operating machinery. The challenge was to restructure the NPD handover ecosystem, transforming dense compliance manuals into usable, action-oriented interfaces that accelerate scale-up and eliminate cognitive friction.

R&D AssumptionShop Floor RealityResulting Friction
The process is finalized, documented, and ready for exact replication.Operators read 50+ pages of dense text while wearing heavy PPE.Longer training, memory reliance, and increased deviation risk during early scale-up.

Behavioral Research

Analyzing operator cognitive load as a new product line reaches the floor.

Information Architecture

Breaking compliance paragraphs into modular, scannable actions.

Tech Transfer Standardization

Creating a scalable handover template between R&D engineers and operators.

presentationSections.label: Problem
presentationSections.content:
The scale-up phase was bottlenecked by cognitive overload.

When a new product reaches manufacturing, operators must rapidly absorb new safety warnings, tooling requirements, and sequential steps.

Legacy NPD documents buried operational data in long, unstructured paragraphs. In sterile cleanrooms, operators wearing double gloves and goggles cannot easily scan or flip through dozens of pages for a tooling parameter. Production was delayed and operators relied on memory. The systemic failure was treating the SOP as a legal archive rather than a live operational tool.

presentationSections.label: Opportunity
presentationSections.content:
Treat the tech transfer document as a user interface.

The SOP is the ultimate UX touchpoint of the NPD lifecycle. Applying visual hierarchy, progressive disclosure, and iconography to the physical document could reduce time-to-market for new drugs.

Opportunity 1

Decouple physical actions from contextual background information to speed execution.

Opportunity 2

Establish a visual language for hazards and tooling so operators can prepare instantly.

Opportunity 3

Standardize the handover protocol so R&D always delivers floor-ready instructions.

presentationSections.label: Solution
presentationSections.content:
A modular, action-driven tech transfer system built for the manufacturing floor.

The redesigned SOP framework supports NPD Scale-Up as a clear operational guide. Its information architecture highlights hazards, separates preparation from execution, and uses visual cues to bypass reading fatigue.

Action-Context Split

What it does: Places physical action left and reasoning right.

Why it matters: Operators can scan actions without R&D background text.

Hazard & Tooling Iconography

What it does: Uses bold icons and high-contrast safety bands.

Why it matters: Critical warnings cannot blend into procedural text.

NPD Handover Template

What it does: Standardizes how R&D authors manufacturing instructions.

Why it matters: Reduces the learning curve for every new product.

presentationSections.label: Core Flows
presentationSections.content:
1. NPD Setup & Pre-Execution

Trigger: An operator receives a newly transferred batch.

Action: Scan required tools and PPE icons.

Response: A standardized legend communicates setup instantly.

Value: Faster batch preparation without hunting through text.

2. Active Floor Execution

Trigger: The new manufacturing sequence begins.

Action: Follow the isolated action column.

Response: One action per row, interrupted by hazard banners.

Value: Lower risk of skipped steps during rollout.

presentationSections.label: Research
presentationSections.content:
Operators were bypassing documents because they were fundamentally unusable in PPE.

Contextual inquiry revealed how operators interacted with legacy SOPs during active new-product runs.

Methods: Contextual Inquiry · Task Analysis · Cognitive Load Assessment

The PPE Barrier

Revealed: Double gloves and goggles restrict page handling and reading.

Implication: Larger type, stronger contrast, and layouts for reduced dexterity.

The Memory Reliance Risk

Revealed: Unusable documents push operators toward memory and word-of-mouth.

Implication: References must be scannable in seconds.

Hidden Hazards

Revealed: Dangerous warnings looked like normal text.

Implication: Color-banded hazards must interrupt the reading pattern.

presentationSections.label: Exploration
presentationSections.content:
Balancing digital ambition with physical cleanroom constraints.

Fully Digital Tablet UI

What it was: Interactive cleanroom iPads for all NPD handovers.

Why promising: Video, dynamic checklists, and instant R&D updates.

Why it changed: Electronics, battery, and sterilization rules made tablets unfeasible in high-risk zones.

Where the direction landed

A hybrid architecture: a printed, laminated document able to survive sterilization, backed by modular information architecture ready for future digital migration.

presentationSections.label: Prototyping and Testing
presentationSections.content:
Validating comprehension under physical floor constraints.

I prototyped SOP layouts across fidelity levels, then printed high-fidelity versions for operator testing under simulated floor conditions and full PPE.

ObservationIteration
Operators initially ignored iconography because they were accustomed to text.Icons were enlarged and a mandatory quick-reference legend was added to the NPD handbook.
The split layout worked, but long runs needed progress tracking.A high-contrast margin was added for manual sign-offs and physical checks.

presentationSections.label: Design Decisions
presentationSections.content:
Prioritizing operational clarity over regulatory tradition.

The Two-Column Architecture

Problem: Operators lost their place in paragraphs. Options: Bullets versus a split table. Decision: Action left, context right. Rationale: Separates what to do from why. Tradeoff: More pages.

Color-Coded Hazard Banners

Problem: New-chemical warnings were overlooked. Options: Bold red text versus full-width banners. Decision: Solid-color warning blocks. Rationale: Breaks visual monotony immediately. Tradeoff: Requires high-quality color printing.

presentationSections.label: Constraints
presentationSections.content:
Designing for zero-tolerance compliance environments.
0

Regulatory Rigidity. There is zero tolerance for altering mandated legal language or breaking audit trails. The response was to preserve every legal requirement while redesigning hierarchy, typography, and presentation for dramatically better usability.

presentationSections.label: Outcome
presentationSections.content:
A scalable framework for operational excellence.

The redesigned SOP and NPD documentation framework was prototyped, validated, and showcased to the Head of Design and senior UX leadership. As a capstone, its foundational architecture was integrated into a larger ongoing strategic initiative shaping the company's future digital transformation.

It established a new standard for communicating complex manufacturing instructions, bridging rigorous R&D science and human-centered execution.

presentationSections.label: Reflection
presentationSections.content:
Information architecture is safety architecture.

Bridging R&D and Manufacturing

The biggest product-development failures often occur during handover, not in the lab. Service design translates engineering into executable action.

The limits of digitization

Sometimes the best solution is laminated paper. Environmental and hardware constraints prevented a digital solution that would have failed on the floor.

A process is only as strong as the interface the frontline worker uses to execute it.

title: Surfing App
subtitle: A mobile telemetry and progression system that helps surfers track wave mechanics through session-based data continuity.
meta: Product Strategy, Interaction Design, Behavioral Research, Rapid Prototyping

presentationSections.label: Overview
presentationSections.content:
How can wave tracking survive the friction of an active surf session?

Surfing relies heavily on environmental intuition. Existing digital tools isolate data to pre-session planning. This project explores a mobile ecosystem designed for the water. It bridges the gap between predictive ocean data and real-time athletic performance.

The challenge was designing an interface that surfers could interact with under extreme environmental constraints without breaking their state of flow. The project also needed to address the high barrier to entry for tourists navigating expensive local coaching and equipment rentals.

Behavioral GapDesign Opportunity
Pre-Entry: Users aggressively check wind and tide data.A single-action lock screen to initiate passive tracking.
Active Session: Extreme glare and water render standard UI unusable.Absolute black-and-white contrast prioritizing a single metric.
Post-Session: Users struggle to recall specific waves.Gamified journaling correlating time-stamped tricks with local wave data.

Behavioral Research

Understanding how surfers interact with telemetry before, during, and after a session.

Environmental Prototyping

Testing interface constraints under high-glare and wet-screen conditions.

Session-Based Continuity

A systemic architecture that preserves context across interrupted interactions.

presentationSections.label: Problem
presentationSections.content:
The disconnect between predictive forecasting and active telemetry.

Surfers lack real-time actionable data on wave mechanics during active sessions. The current ecosystem forces users to check their phones strictly pre-entry. Once they are in the water, the feedback loop breaks.

This leaves a blind spot in performance tracking. Surfers rely on memory and post-session analysis rather than in-the-moment adjustments. Beyond the water, tourists and beginners face high friction on land. Finding verified equipment and affordable coaching in coastal towns often involves hidden charges and fragmented local networks.

The core issue was not a lack of data. The issue was the inability to safely deliver that data in a hostile physical environment while supporting the user's broader journey.

presentationSections.label: Opportunity
presentationSections.content:
Shift telemetry from pre-session planning to active session tracking.

I realized the interface needed to stop competing with the physical environment and start adapting to it. The strategic opportunity was to build a system that required minimal visual attention while delivering maximum contextual value, doubling as a digital coach.

Opportunity 1

Minimize active input requirements through passive biometric and GPS tracking.

Opportunity 2

Utilize high-contrast glanceable UI for high-glare environments.

Opportunity 3

Build a retention loop through integrated progression journaling and localized equipment rentals.

presentationSections.label: Solution
presentationSections.content:
An interruption-tolerant tracking system built for the water.

The Surfing App is a conceptual mobile platform that tracks wave mechanics and physical performance seamlessly. It uses a high-contrast interface designed specifically for minimal interaction.

By structuring the architecture around session-based continuity, the app ensures that no context is lost when navigating away from core tasks or when the device auto-locks in the water. It also functions as a long-term data collection tool to study unknown wave patterns through aggregated tourist session logs.

Session-Based Continuity

What it does: Preserves active state data without manual saves.

Why it matters: Short, interrupted interactions cannot afford lost context.

Glanceable Telemetry

What it does: Prioritizes single-metric visualization.

Why it matters: Sunlight and water obscure complex layouts.

Progression & Classes

What it does: Logs tricks, personal bests, and video tutorials.

Why it matters: It creates a digital coaching alternative.

Equipment Marketplace

What it does: Connects users to local shops.

Why it matters: It removes hidden-charge friction for tourists.

presentationSections.label: Core Flows
presentationSections.content:
1. Session Setup

Trigger: A new surf session begins.

Action: The user defines location and targets with one swipe.

Response: The app locks for water use and starts background telemetry.

Value: Prevents pre-entry friction and accidental touches.

2. Skill Progression Logging

Trigger: The user returns to land.

Action: They review telemetry and log named tricks.

Response: Timestamps are cross-referenced with local wave data.

Value: Builds a personal journal and maps local wave behavior.

presentationSections.label: Research
presentationSections.content:
Users check their phones strictly pre-entry.

To understand aquatic tech friction, I combined Synthetic Users for rapid AI-simulated interviews with contextual inquiry and diary studies. Hotjar AI was used to parse quantitative behavioral data.

Methods: Contextual Inquiry · Diary Studies · Synthetic User AI Testing · Quantitative Behavioral Parsing

The Pre-Entry Wall

Revealed: Interfaces are unusable when wet.

Implication: An aquatic lock state with passive tracking.

The Coaching Cost Barrier

Revealed: Non-locals face steep costs and hidden charges.

Implication: Embedded tutorials and a trusted rental module.

The Voice UI Trap

Revealed: Voice becomes muffled and unreliable in the ocean.

Implication: Reject audio trends for high-contrast visual cues.

presentationSections.label: Exploration
presentationSections.content:
Balancing data density with environmental constraints.

Audio-First Feedback

What it was: Waterproof earbuds delivering wave stats via an AI agent.

Why promising: It bypassed screen visibility.

Why it changed: Ocean acoustics caused constant voice-model failure and repetition.

High-Density Dashboard

What it was: Wind, swell, and tide shown simultaneously.

Why promising: Total environmental control.

Why it changed: Extreme cognitive overload during active sessions.

Where the direction landed

A simplified high-contrast interface that prioritizes one metric and uses session-based architecture to remember context.

presentationSections.label: Prototyping and Testing
presentationSections.content:
Testing UI legibility and form factors under physical stress.

Due to the strict eight-week timeline, I bypassed extensive low-fidelity wireframes. I used Crazy Eights for rapid ideation, Relume for structural IA, and moved directly into mid-fidelity greyscale Figma prototypes.

Motion & Contrast

What happened: Stakeholders reported motion sickness and visual hallucinations.

What it meant: Motion-specific WCAG calibration was required.

What changed: The palette was adjusted to reduce visual vibration.

Foldable Hardware

What happened: A folded Samsung phone broke standard tap targets.

What it meant: Form factors radically alter aquatic interaction.

What changed: Responsive state management became a critical next phase while v1 remained fixed.

presentationSections.label: Design Decisions
presentationSections.content:
The final design was shaped by environmental realities.

Session-Based Continuity

Problem: Auto-lock loses context. Decision: The active state persists until manually stopped. Rationale: It mirrors continuous physical activity. Tradeoff: More complex backend state logic.

Bypassing AI Voice UI

Problem: Screen access is difficult while paddling. Decision: Voice was dropped for high-contrast minimal UI. Rationale: Ocean acoustics are unreliable. Tradeoff: Occasional glances remain necessary.

Embedded Market Ecosystem

Problem: Tourists face hidden coaching and rental charges. Decision: Add rentals and embedded classes. Rationale: It solves a direct pain point and creates retention. Tradeoff: Increased IA scope.

presentationSections.label: Constraints
presentationSections.content:
Designing for an interface that is wet, glaring, and moving.

Eight-Week Time Crunch

V1 was locked to one viewport so the core session logic could be resolved; foldable edge cases were documented for later.

High Glare

Subtle grayscales were eliminated in favor of absolute black-and-white contrast.

Touch Inaccuracy

Small tap targets were replaced with large edge-to-edge swipe zones.

presentationSections.label: Outcome
presentationSections.content:
A validated concept ready for higher-fidelity development.

The project established a viable interaction model for aquatic environments. Re-interviewing the initial user base showed strong optimism. Users were highly receptive to progression journaling and equipment rentals that bypass high-cost coaching. The concept also established a long-term data trajectory for studying localized wave patterns through aggregated tourist session logs.

presentationSections.label: Reflection
presentationSections.content:
Moving from screen-led to context-led design.

Scoping against trends

Voice AI was a major trend, but testing proved it would fail in the ocean. The best technology is the one that works in the user's environment.

Designing for hostile environments

The context forced decorative UI away; every pixel had to serve a functional purpose.

Systems thinking in state management

Good UX is also how the system remembers where the user was. Session continuity became the product anchor.

The best digital architecture adapts to human behavior rather than forcing humans to adapt to the screen.

caseSections.label: Context & Friction
caseSections.content:
Surfing relies heavily on environmental intuition, yet existing digital tools isolate telemetry data to pre-session planning.

Surfers check their phones on the beach, but once they enter the water, the feedback loop breaks.

This project explores an interruption-tolerant mobile ecosystem designed for the hostile environment of the ocean. The challenge was designing an interface that surfers could interact with under extreme physical constraints (glare, water, motion) without breaking their state of flow, while simultaneously solving the high barrier to entry for tourists navigating expensive local coaching networks.

caseSections.label: Systems Analysis
caseSections.content:
Behavioral Gap Analysis: The Pre-Entry Wall

Using Synthetic Users for rapid AI-simulated interviews, followed by contextual field studies, I mapped the complete user journey to identify where the data loop failed.

Session PhaseUser BehaviorSystem FrictionThe Design Opportunity
Pre-EntryAggressively checks wind, tide, and swell data.High cognitive load; attempting to memorize patterns.Session Setup Swipe: A single-action, high-contrast lock screen that initiates passive background telemetry.
Active SessionRelies entirely on physical intuition; device is locked or left behind.Wet screens and extreme glare render standard UI completely unusable.Glanceable Architecture: Absolute black-and-white contrast prioritizing a single metric per screen; edge-to-edge swipe targets.
Post-SessionAttempts to recall specific waves or tricks to track progression.Memory degradation; tourists lack local knowledge to benchmark against.Gamified Progression Journaling: Correlating time-stamped tricks with localized wave data to map unknown patterns.

caseSections.label: Testing & Constraints
caseSections.content:
Testing Pivots & The Reality of the Environment

Because of the tight 8-week timeline, I moved rapidly from "Crazy Eights" ideation directly into mid-fidelity greyscale testing in Figma to stress-test the interaction models.

Concept TestedUser / Environmental FeedbackStrategic Pivot
Voice AI (Agentic Feedback)Users reported their own voices sound muffled or trapped in their heads while surfing. Audio models failed against wave noise.Abandoned Voice UI: Despite the 2024 trend of AI agents, I stripped out voice entirely in favor of high-contrast visual continuity.
High-Contrast Motion UISenior stakeholders noted the specific color contrasts combined with moving water induced motion sickness (hallucinations).WCAG Motion Calibration: Recalibrated the color system and contrast ratios to meet strict accessibility standards for aquatic motion.
Hardware AgnosticismA user tested the prototype on a folding Samsung flip phone, completely breaking the standard tap targets.Responsive Constraints: Acknowledged the severe impact of unique form factors on touch targets, logging it as a critical v2 requirement while locking v1 to a standard viewport.

caseSections.label: Solution Architecture
caseSections.content:
The Architecture of Session-Based Continuity

Good UX is not just about the screen you are on; it is about how the system remembers where you were. I engineered the app around Session-Based Continuity. Information does not carry over unnecessarily, but the active state never resets until manually stopped.

This architecture solved the core problem of aquatic lockouts. It allowed for the integration of a localized equipment marketplace and video coaching module—bypassing expensive local tourist traps—by keeping the user anchored in a single, continuous retention loop from the beach, to the water, and back to the journal.

caseSections.label: Outcome & Reflection
caseSections.content: The final system turns a fragmented pre-session tool into one interruption-tolerant journey: setup on the beach, passive continuity in the water, and meaningful progression afterward.

How can wave tracking survive the friction of an active surf session?

Surfing depends heavily on environmental intuition. Most digital surf tools help users prepare before entering the water, but the moment the session begins, the feedback loop breaks.

This project explores a mobile ecosystem designed around that gap. It connects predictive ocean data, active session tracking, personal progression, and local surf support into one continuous experience.

The challenge was not simply to design another sports-tracking app. It was to design an interface that could survive glare, water, motion, interrupted attention, and the physical rhythm of surfing without breaking the user’s state of flow.

Glanceable Telemetry

flows.content:
The experience is built around two high-friction moments: entering the water and returning from it.

The core flows were designed to reduce interaction during the session and move deeper reflection to the moment after the surfer returns to land.

Flow 1: Session Setup

Trigger: The user initiates a new surf session on the beach.

Action: The user defines location and targets with a simple setup interaction.

System response: The app locks the screen for water use and begins background telemetry.

Value: It removes pre-entry friction and prevents accidental touches in the water.

Flow 2: Skill Progression Logging

Trigger: The user completes a session and returns to land.

Action: The user reviews telemetry and logs named tricks.

System response: The app connects trick timestamps with localized wave-pattern data.

Value: It builds a personal progression journal and contributes to long-term wave behavior mapping.

Flow 3: Equipment and Learning Support

Trigger: A tourist or beginner needs gear, lessons, or skill guidance.

Action: The user browses trusted rental options or embedded learning content.

System response: The app surfaces localized support without relying on informal networks.

Value: It reduces the cost and trust barrier around surf coaching and rentals.

Flow visual slot: journey map, app flow diagram, session loop animation, or wireflow

research.content:
Users checked their phones before entering the water, then abandoned the interface completely.

To understand the friction points of aquatic tech use, the research combined rapid early validation with deeper behavioral observation.

Synthetic Users were used to generate early interview patterns and pressure-test assumptions. These were followed by contextual inquiry and diary-style observation to understand how surfers actually behave before, during, and after sessions.

Method: Contextual Inquiry

Used to understand the physical and environmental conditions around surf preparation, device use, and session entry.

Method: Diary Studies

Used to observe patterns across sessions rather than relying only on one-time recall.

Method: Synthetic User AI Testing

Used for rapid early validation and to identify possible friction points before moving into grounded research.

Method: Quantitative Behavioral Parsing

Used to make sense of repeated behavioral patterns and translate them into product decisions.

Research visual slot: observation notes, journey mapping, research synthesis clusters, or insight cards

The Pre-Entry Wall

Users leave devices behind because current interfaces are not usable when wet. The design implication was clear: the app needed an aquatic lock state and passive tracking capabilities.

The Coaching Cost Barrier

Tourists and beginners often navigate steep costs, hidden charges, and unreliable local networks. This shaped the decision to include tutorials and trusted rental access.

The Voice UI Trap

Voice interaction seemed relevant at first, but the surfing environment made it unreliable. The final interface avoids voice input and depends on visual clarity instead.

formFactors.content:
The project shifted from feature density to environmental restraint.

Early exploration focused on how much information the app should expose during a session. The strongest direction was not the one with the most features, but the one that asked the least from the user while they were physically engaged with the water.

Audio-First Feedback

What it was: A waterproof earbud-based flow that delivered wave stats through an AI voice layer.

Why it seemed promising: It bypassed the screen visibility problem completely.

Why it changed: Ocean acoustics made voice input and feedback unreliable. Repeating commands would break concentration and increase frustration.

High-Density Dashboard

What it was: A data-heavy screen showing wind, swell, tide, and performance metrics together.

Why it seemed promising: It gave the user more control over environmental variables.

Why it changed: It caused too much cognitive load during the session and became harder to read in glare and motion.

Simplified Visual Telemetry

Where the direction landed: The final direction prioritizes one metric at a time through a high-contrast interface, while the system architecture remembers the larger session context in the background.

Exploration visual slot: rejected voice UI concept, dense dashboard concept, simplified telemetry comparison

prototyping.content:
Testing revealed that visibility was not only about contrast. It was about motion, context, and device behavior.

Due to the eight-week timeline, the project moved quickly from ideation into mid-fidelity prototyping. Crazy Eights was used for rapid concept generation, Relume supported early information architecture, and Figma was used to build testable greyscale prototypes.

The goal was not to perfect visual design early. It was to expose the interaction model to physical and behavioral stress as quickly as possible.

Prototype visual slot: Figma mid-fidelity screens, greyscale flow, or before-after interface iterations

Testing Insight 1: High contrast can still create discomfort

Senior stakeholders noted that the initial high-contrast palette could induce motion discomfort or visual vibration in moving water. The color system was recalibrated to reduce harshness while retaining legibility.

Testing Insight 2: Hardware variation changes the interaction model

One user attempted to interact with the prototype on a folded Samsung flip phone. This revealed that aquatic hardware constraints go beyond waterproofing. Form factor, viewport, and touch target behavior need to be treated as future design requirements.

Testing Insight 3: Scope had to protect the core interaction

The first version remained locked to a standard viewport so the session logic could be resolved clearly before expanding into responsive edge cases.

decisions.content:
The final design was shaped by environmental realities, not interface trends.

Decision 1: Preserve the session until the user ends it

Problem: Users frequently lose context when an app auto-locks, reloads, or resets during physical activity.

Options considered: Standard app state management versus persistent background session logic.

Final decision: The active state remains continuous until manually stopped.

Rationale: This mirrors the mental model of surfing as one continuous physical session.

Tradeoff: It requires more complex backend state logic.

Decision 2: Remove AI voice interaction

Problem: Users cannot easily look at screens while paddling or moving through water.

Options considered: Voice agents versus high-contrast visual feedback.

Final decision: Voice interaction was removed entirely.

Rationale: Muffled acoustics and ocean noise made voice models too unreliable for this context.

Tradeoff: The user still needs occasional visual attention, but the system avoids misinterpreted commands.

Decision 3: Include the market ecosystem lightly

Problem: Tourists face hidden charges when seeking coaching or renting surf equipment.

Options considered: A pure telemetry app versus an integrated support ecosystem.

Final decision: The app includes a lightweight rental and embedded video class module.

Rationale: It responds to a real pain point while giving the product a stronger retention loop.

Tradeoff: It increases the information architecture scope.

Design decision visual slot: system logic diagram, voice UI rejection diagram, or feature tradeoff matrix

hardware.content:
Designing for an interface that is wet, glaring, and moving.

The interface had to respond to a hostile environment. The screen was not treated as a stable surface. It was treated as something affected by water, glare, inaccurate touch, interruptions, and body movement.

Eight-Week Time Constraint

The timeline limited the ability to design a fully responsive ecosystem from day one. The first version stayed locked to a single viewport so the core session logic could be resolved well.

High Glare

Sunlight makes subtle UI elements disappear. The interface removed soft grayscale dependence and moved toward stronger contrast and clearer hierarchy.

Touch Inaccuracy

Wet fingers and screens increase mis-taps. Standard tap targets were replaced by larger, simpler interaction zones where possible.

Constraint visual slot: glare test, wet-screen touch diagram, hardware stress states, or responsive notes

reflection.content:
Moving from screen-led to context-led design.

Scoping against trends

This project reinforced the importance of ignoring industry trends when the context demands it. Voice AI was a strong trend during the project, but the ocean made it unreliable. The best technology was not the most current one. It was the one that worked in the user’s environment.

Designing for hostile environments

The surfing context forced the interface to become more disciplined. Decorative UI had to be stripped away because every pixel needed to support visibility, orientation, or action.

Systems thinking in state management

The strongest learning was that good UX is not only about the screen in front of the user. It is also about how the system remembers what the user was doing. Session-based continuity became the anchor of the entire product.

This project clarified a larger design belief: digital architecture should adapt to human behavior, instead of forcing people to adapt to the screen.

title: Kaari
subtitle: A service ecosystem and physical hardware product that connects artisans directly to buyers across language barriers.
pageTitle: Kaari Service Design Ecosystem | Areen Pednekar
metaDescription: A comprehensive service design and hardware case study exploring how native audio terminals and integrated logistics can bypass middlemen in the artisanal craft sector.
previewText: Connecting buyers directly to craftsmen by replacing screens with a dust-resistant native-audio terminal.
meta: Service Designer — Client app flows, Artisan backend, CAD modeling, Rapid prototyping
Service Design, Industrial Design, Ethnography, Information Architecture

presentationSections.label: Overview
presentationSections.content:
How do you digitize an artisan's business without forcing them to become digital experts?

The artisanal supply chain is dominated by middlemen. Buyers, such as design students and boutique owners, struggle to communicate directly with karigars (craftsmen) due to severe language barriers and logistical friction. Kaari is a holistic service design intervention bridging the gap between modern e-commerce and traditional, dusty workshops.

The challenge was designing a dual-sided digital platform paired with a physical hardware device that speaks the artisan's native language, completely rendering the broker obsolete.

Traditional Broker ModelKaari Ecosystem
Brokers travel to workshops to translate order intake.Digital spec sheets are translated instantly via API.
Brokers manually collect and ship for a premium.Porter or Dunzo is dispatched directly to the workshop.
Artisans retain 40–50% of project value.Artisans retain the full fabrication value.
40–50%

The share of true project value artisans traditionally retain when a broker controls translation and logistics.

Ethnographic Research

Spending time in karigar workshops to understand physical and linguistic constraints.

Hardware Prototyping

Designing and 3D printing a dust-resistant audio terminal for the workshop floor.

Ecosystem Design

Connecting buyer apps, artisan hardware, and third-party logistics into one seamless service.

presentationSections.label: Problem
presentationSections.content:
Language barriers create a dependency on brokers who erode artisan profits.

When buyers from large export houses or design schools need custom work, they cannot easily communicate with the actual craftsmen. The karigars rely heavily on their native language and traditional manual workflows. This forces the introduction of a middleman to translate and manage orders.

This broker takes a massive percentage of the profit. The deeper issue was that existing digital platforms assumed high digital literacy and English proficiency, making them useless on a noisy, dusty workshop floor.

presentationSections.label: Opportunity
presentationSections.content:
Build technology that adapts to the workshop, not the other way around.

caseSections.label: Context & Friction
caseSections.content:
The artisanal supply chain is fundamentally broken by a reliance on middlemen.

Buyers—such as design students, boutique owners, and export houses—struggle to communicate directly with karigars (craftsmen) due to severe language barriers and logistical friction. Consequently, brokers step in, taking a massive percentage of the profit simply to act as translators and shippers.

Kaari is a holistic service design intervention that bridges the gap between modern e-commerce and traditional, dusty workshops. The challenge was not just building a digital app, but designing a dual-sided platform paired with a physical hardware device that speaks the artisan's native language—rendering the broker entirely obsolete without forcing the artisan to become a digital expert.

The artisan accepts the job via a tactile, dust-proof button. Once fabrication is complete, hitting a second tactile trigger pings the Dunzo/Porter API, dispatching a driver for final-mile logistics.

How do you digitize an artisan's business without forcing them to become digital experts?

The artisanal supply chain is dominated by middlemen. Buyers, such as design students and boutique owners, struggle to communicate directly with karigars (craftsmen) due to severe language barriers and logistical friction. Kaari is a holistic service design intervention bridging the gap between modern e-commerce and traditional, dusty workshops.

The challenge was designing a dual-sided digital platform paired with a physical hardware device that speaks the artisan's native language, completely rendering the broker obsolete.

Ethnographic Research

Spending time in karigar workshops to understand physical and linguistic constraints.

Hardware Prototyping

Designing and 3D-printing a dust-resistant audio terminal for the workshop floor.

Ecosystem Design

Connecting buyer apps, artisan hardware, and third-party logistics into one seamless service.

Language barriers create a dependency on brokers who erode artisan profits.

When buyers from large export houses or design schools need custom work, they cannot easily communicate with the actual craftsmen. The karigars rely heavily on their native language and traditional manual workflows. This forces the introduction of a middleman to translate and manage orders.

This broker ends up taking a massive percentage of the profit. The visible symptom was a lack of direct digital commerce for artisans. The deeper underlying issue was that existing digital platforms assumed high digital literacy and English proficiency, making them entirely useless on a noisy, dusty workshop floor.

Build technology that adapts to the workshop, not the other way around.

Observing karigars successfully use audio-based payment confirmation boxes revealed a massive opportunity. We could use that exact mental model for order management, replacing screens with sound.

Opportunity 1

Translate digital text orders into native audio announcements on the workshop floor.

Opportunity 2

Create a dual-interface ecosystem where buyers use a modern app and artisans use a rugged hardware terminal.

Opportunity 3

Unify the fragmented delivery process by integrating third-party logistics APIs.

A combined hardware and software service that translates orders into spoken native dialects.

flows.content:
The Custom Order Request

Trigger: A buyer needs a custom piece fabricated.

Action: The user inputs specifications, reference images, and material requests into the Kaari app.

System response: The system structures the request and routes it to an appropriate artisan's queue.

Value: It standardizes custom requests without requiring a broker to negotiate terms.

The Artisan Hardware Handoff

Trigger: A new order reaches the artisan's digital queue.

Action: The physical terminal lights up and announces the order details out loud in the artisan's native language.

System response: The artisan accepts the job via a tactile button on the device.

Value: It respects the craftsman's existing technological comfort zone and keeps them focused on their physical labor.

Automated Logistics Dispatch

Trigger: The artisan marks the physical product as complete on the terminal.

Action: The system automatically pings a third-party delivery partner.

System response: A driver is dispatched directly to the workshop for pickup and delivery to the buyer.

Value: It removes the final logistical hurdle, making the artisan fully independent.

research.content:
The most valuable insights came from the workshop floor, not a survey.

The research phase relied on deep ethnography. We went directly into the homes and workspaces of karigars, while also conducting qualitative interviews with fashion, product, and interior design students who frequently source artisanal work.

Methods Used

Contextual Inquiry & Field Studies

User Interviews

Usability Testing

The Audio Precedent

What it revealed: Artisans were highly comfortable with audio-based smart devices because they do not require stopping manual labor to read a screen.

Design implication: Order management needed a hardware component that relied on native audio feedback rather than a purely screen-based UI.

The Middleman Tax

What it revealed: Middlemen exist primarily to bridge the language and logistics gap, not to add value to the craft itself.

Design implication: The service needed integrated translation and automated delivery to render the middleman obsolete.

The Environmental Reality

What it revealed: Standard electronics fail or degrade quickly in artisan workshops due to severe dust and heat.

formFactors.content:
Engineering a form factor for heat, dust, and heavy use.

Screen-Heavy Tablet App

What it was: A ruggedized tablet given to artisans to manage their digital storefront.

Why it seemed promising: It allowed for high information density and image viewing.

Why it changed, failed, or evolved: Contextual testing showed artisans could not easily wipe their hands to tap screens constantly. It interrupted their actual craft.

Exposed Speaker Terminal

What it was: A highly perforated smart speaker design.

Why it seemed promising: It maximized audio clarity for the noisy workshop.

Why it changed, failed, or evolved: Mockups left in the workshop collected severe dust in the speaker grille, threatening the internal mechanics.

Where the direction landed

I modeled and 3D-printed a sleek, sealed hardware terminal. It prioritized thermal management and a dust-resistant shell, utilizing minimal tactile buttons and a protected audio output. App exploration focused on earthy tones and highly accessible digital ID integrations to build trust.

prototyping.content:
Validating physical durability and digital accessibility.

The prototyping phase was split between testing the digital application flows with buyers and testing the physical hardware mockups in real artisan environments. I utilized CAD to print structural mockups specifically for environmental stress testing.

Workshop Dust Testing

What happened: We left physical form mockups in active workshops for several days.

What it meant: Micro-particles and dust seeped into standard device seams, confirming that typical consumer electronics would not survive.

What changed in the design: I adjusted the CAD models to create a sleeker, sealed form factor that battled dust accumulation while managing heat dissipation.

Artisan Onboarding Testing

What happened: Early app testing revealed friction during the artisan onboarding process.

What it meant: Traditional form-filling was too tedious for users who preferred physical labor over digital admin.

What changed in the design: We pivoted to integrate automated national ID verification (DigiLocker) to make digital onboarding almost instantaneous.

Prototype visual slot: physical CAD models and 3D prints on a workshop table being tested for dust

decisions.content:
The final ecosystem was shaped by physical realities, not just digital best practices.

Decision 1: Designing Hardware, Not Just Software

Problem: An app alone could not bridge the usability gap on a workshop floor.

Options considered: An artisan-facing mobile app versus a dedicated physical device.

Final decision: Built a bespoke audio hardware terminal.

Rationale: It matched the existing mental model of payment announcers and kept the artisan's hands free.

Tradeoff: It massively increased the complexity of the project by introducing industrial design and manufacturing constraints.

Decision 2: Native Audio Translation

Problem: Buyers and karigars do not speak the same languages.

Options considered: In-app text translation versus localized audio announcements.

Final decision: The hardware device speaks orders out loud in local dialects.

Rationale: It entirely removes the need for literacy or screen time to understand an incoming order.

Tradeoff: Required complex backend integrations for real-time localized text-to-speech.

Decision 3: Outsourcing Logistics

Problem: Artisans do not have time to manage shipping and delivery.

Options considered: Building an internal tracking system versus third-party API integration.

Final decision: Integrated services like Dunzo and Porter directly into the app.

Rationale: It leveraged existing infrastructure to automate the final mile, removing the logistical middleman.

Tradeoff: The service relies heavily on the API reliability of third-party delivery partners.

hardware.content:
Designing ahead of the available technological infrastructure.

API Limitations in 2023

Why it mattered: At the time of development, infrastructure like DigiLocker was still emerging, making seamless digital ID handoffs complex to execute perfectly in a live build.

How the design responded: We had to pitch the integration as a forward-looking architectural concept, designing the user flow for how the APIs would eventually behave at scale rather than limiting the vision to what was strictly available that month.

A comprehensive ecosystem bridging the digital and physical divide.

Kaari culminated in a thoroughly validated service ecosystem featuring a tested digital application and a 3D-printed hardware prototype. The project successfully mapped a realistic route to bypass industry middlemen, empowering artisans to retain their margins while giving buyers direct access to custom craft.

Detail visual slot: close-up render of the final hardware form factor emphasizing the sealed, dust-resistant design

reflection.content:
Service design is about observing invisible systems.

Empathy requires physical presence

You cannot design for an artisan by sitting behind a screen. Being physically present in their workstations, seeing the dust, and hearing the noise fundamentally changed my understanding of what makes a product "usable."

The hardware-software bridge

This project shifted my perspective from pure digital UI to holistic service design. A digital app is useless if the physical environment rejects it. Creating hardware to act as a bridge was the only way to make the software successful.

Kaari cemented my approach to design. True innovation happens when you stop forcing users to learn your interface, and instead build your interface to survive their reality.

title: Koya
subtitle: A furniture collection and brand identity that brings durable, handcrafted brutalism to young Indian professionals.
pageTitle: Koya Industrial Design & Branding | Areen Pednekar
metaDescription: A comprehensive industrial design and branding case study exploring brutalist furniture fabrication, material honesty, and cross-disciplinary brand strategy.
previewText: Balancing the raw aesthetic of sheet metal and dark oak to create durable, monolithic statement pieces.
meta: Industrial Designer — Prototyping, 3D Modeling, Material Sourcing
Industrial Design, Brand Strategy, Rapid Prototyping, Fabrication

presentationSections.label: Overview
presentationSections.content:
How do you design furniture that survives the transient lifestyle of a young professional?

Young professionals moving to hubs like Mumbai and Bangalore default to flat-pack furniture. While accessible, it lacks a bold identity and degrades rapidly through repeated assembly and disassembly. Koya is an industrial design and branding intervention that introduces durable, handmade brutalism to this demographic.

The challenge was balancing the raw, unrefined aesthetic of metal and dark wood with the functional needs of modern apartment living, while establishing a highly distinct brand language that stands out in a saturated market.

Material Strategy

Identifying the exact contrast between warm dark oak and cold sheet metal.

Brand Identity

Creating a stark, structural graphic language that mirrors the physical furniture.

Industrial Fabrication

Transitioning from CAD models to 1:1 scale manufacturing with local karigars.

presentationSections.label: Problem
presentationSections.content:
Flat-pack furniture wears out, and luxury furniture is inaccessible.

The current market for young professionals in India forces a compromise. They either buy mass-produced, flimsy particle board furniture that chips during apartment moves, or they are priced out of high-end, durable wooden pieces.

The visible symptom is a cycle of disposable furniture. The deeper issue is the lack of a middle ground. There was no brand offering a bold, permanent aesthetic that justified a slightly higher price point through sheer durability and material honesty.

presentationSections.label: Opportunity
presentationSections.content:
Establish a new category of accessible brutalism.

Observing the emerging trend of minimalism mixed with raw materials, we identified a gap in the Indian market. Users wanted the warmth of traditional woods combined with the cold, industrial feel of modern metalwork.

Opportunity 1

Use raw, non-processed materials to eliminate the wear and tear of flat-pack joints.

Opportunity 2

Build an entire brand catalog and packaging ecosystem to elevate the perceived value of the product.

Opportunity 3

Blend fashion, interior, communication, and product design into a holistic lifestyle brand.

presentationSections.label: Solution
presentationSections.content:
A catalog of handmade, brutalist furniture anchored by a strong visual identity.

Koya is a complete product and brand ecosystem. It features a line of furniture designed to last lifetimes rather than lease terms. The catalog includes central coffee tables, entrance mirrors, and console units that function as structural statement pieces.

Honest Materiality

What it does: Uses solid rosewood and raw metal instead of veneers.

Why it matters: Delivers decades of structural integrity while embracing brutalism.

Monolithic Form Factor

What it does: Uses heavy 90-degree metal bends for storage and structure.

Why it matters: Removes user assembly and weak joints.

Unified Brand Ecosystem

What it does: Aligns the products with bespoke packaging and graphic identity.

Why it matters: Positions the collection as a premium lifestyle choice.

presentationSections.label: Branding
presentationSections.content:
Translating raw materials into a graphic language.

Koya required a brand identity as bold as its physical materials. The visual language mirrors the products: stark, textured, and unapologetic.

Brand ElementVisual Translation
Logo MarkCustom typography with architectural cuts mirroring sharp 90-degree sheet-metal bends.
Color PaletteEarthy warm browns set against industrial greys and absolute blacks.
CollateralTextured business cards and bold minimalist packaging that preview the furniture's tactile character.

presentationSections.label: Product Lifecycle
presentationSections.content:
From conceptual sketches to the workshop floor.

Because this was a physical product, the process required moving rapidly from digital space into physical materials.

1. Ideation and CAD

We defined the structural language in 3D, balancing heavy metal bases with floating wooden tops before sourcing material.

2. Miniature Mockups

Scaled models of tables and mirror consoles helped evaluate spatial balance and room dynamics before heavy fabrication.

3. True-Scale Fabrication

Local craftsmen helped build the entrance console while we navigated thick metal bends and integrated electronics.

presentationSections.label: Research
presentationSections.content:
The shift toward minimal brutalism.

Research focused on material trends and the transient lifestyles of young professionals in metro cities. We observed fatigue with generic Scandinavian minimalism and a rising demand for bold, anchoring pieces.

Methods: Market Analysis · Trend Forecasting · User Interviews

The Assembly Fatigue

Revealed: Assembly is frustrating and joints fail after moves.

Implication: Fully formed monolithic structures.

The Material Contrast

Revealed: Users want dark-wood warmth with cold modern metal.

Implication: Build the brand around this intersection.

The Statement Piece

Revealed: Young renters prefer one premium anchor piece.

Implication: Each design must stand alone in a sparse apartment.

presentationSections.label: Prototyping and Testing
presentationSections.content:
Refining the physical ergonomics of sheet metal.

We built a 1:1 true-scale prototype of the entrance table with a wooden top, integrated working light, and 90-degree bent metal base for books and everyday carry. Testing focused on physical interaction, texture, and safety.

ObservationIteration
Raw sheet-metal edges were too sharp for a living space.The edges were sanded and radiused for safe daily interaction.
The raw wood felt unfinished and lacked a premium tactile quality.A deep polish created a rich contrast against the matte metal.

presentationSections.label: Design Decisions
presentationSections.content:
Balancing aesthetic aggression with domestic comfort.

Material Selection

Problem: Particle board lacks durability. Options: High-grade plywood versus solid wood and metal. Decision: Solid dark wood with heavy sheet metal. Rationale: Structural longevity and a brutalist identity. Tradeoff: Higher manufacturing and retail cost.

The Monolithic Form

Problem: Complex assembly fails over time. Options: Modular joints versus fixed bends. Decision: Heavy 90-degree bends as the structural foundation. Rationale: Zero user assembly and a strong silhouette. Tradeoff: Greater weight and shipping complexity.

presentationSections.label: Constraints
presentationSections.content:
Fabricating without industrial manufacturing lines.
1:1

Local Sourcing and Craftsmanship. Without mass-production facilities or automated metal-bending machines, the team leaned into a handmade aesthetic. Minor metalwork and polishing imperfections became part of the raw brutalist identity.

presentationSections.label: Outcome
presentationSections.content:
A highly tactile product ready for market presentation.

The project culminated in a fully functional, true-scale entrance-table prototype with integrated lighting. Miniature mockups were completed for the rest of the catalog, alongside a comprehensive photoshoot and finalized brand book. The project proved that a bold brutalist aesthetic could be adapted for the Indian professional market.

presentationSections.label: Reflection
presentationSections.content:
The power of a cross-disciplinary team.

Harmonizing perspectives

Working with fashion, interior, and communication designers showed that a product exists inside a brand ecosystem and a curated room. Every discipline elevated the others.

Material honesty

The contrast between polished wood and raw metal became the identity, requiring very little decorative intervention.

Koya proved that physical product design is most successful when treated as a holistic lifestyle intervention rather than just a functional object.
